auxiliary_material: The study utilized untargeted metabolomics and bile acid profiling via LC-MS/MS on sera from 43 patients, with current analysis focusing on paired samples from high fiber (n=6) and control (n=8) arms during equilibration vs week 1-4. The human trial observed a numerically higher response rate in the high fiber arm. The mouse model involved n=5 recipients per group. The study duration was up to 10 weeks with fiber ramped from 30 g/d to 50 g/d in the intervention arm.

The abstract notes early results revealed promising improvements in treatment outcomes with the high fiber diet intervention but focuses primarily on systemic immunity profiling rather than detailed human microbiome compositional analysis. The study highlights that circulating monocyte levels are known to negatively correlate with ICB response and warrants further mechanistic study on dietary fiber mediated regulation of peripheral immunity. Subgroup analysis indicated findings were more prominent in those receiving combination nivolumab + ipilimumab compared to monotherapy, though sample sizes were small (n=3 vs n=7).

The study outlines specific eligibility criteria relevant to microbiome integrity, such as excluding patients with recent antibiotic use (within 21 days), active inflammatory bowel disease, or prior bariatric surgery that disrupts the gastrointestinal lumen. It describes the intervention logistics, including a 1-week equilibration period and meals prepared by a Bionutrition Core to ensure isocaloric and macronutrient-controlled conditions. The authors hypothesize a mechanism where dietary fiber increases short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), which may enhance T-cell memory potential via epigenetic regulation, providing a theoretical framework for the mediation analysis planned in future results.
note: The gap judgment and ready writing material are reported separately.
outline_action: Use this material to document that the DIET trial has identified microbiome-mediated functional changes (bile acid biotransformation) associated with dietary intervention and ICB response. Cite the mouse FMT data as supporting evidence for the mechanistic link. In the gap analysis, note that specific taxa data and formal statistical mediation analysis of microbiome-to-clinical outcomes in humans are not detailed in this abstract, indicating a need to consult full-text publications or companion reports for complete mediation statistics.

query_audits.query_text: DIET trial NCT04645680 microbiome mediation analysis high fiber diet immunotherapy melanoma

Has the DIET trial (NCT04645680) published microbiome sequencing data showing specific bacterial taxa or metabolic pathway changes that mediate the clinical efficacy of high-fiber diet intervention in melanoma patients receiving immune checkpoint blockade?

remaining_gap: This abstract does not list specific gut microbiome taxa compositional changes associated with the intervention in the human cohort, focusing instead on serum metabolite proxies for microbiome function. It does not explicitly report a statistical mediation analysis linking specific microbiome changes (taxa or functional pathways) to clinical outcomes (ORR, PFS, OS) in the human participants, though it links bile acid profiles to response in mouse models and notes numerical response differences in humans. There is no explicit statement that microbiome mediation data is pending or unavailable, but the reported data prioritizes metabolic profiling over microbiome sequencing results.
